title: Striving to understand
hookLine: a qualified scholar's effort to reach a ruling

lines: THOSE ABLE TO DRAW IT OUT.
cards: News reaches a town: something about safety, or something about danger, and people pass it along at once, before anyone has checked what it means. The Qur'an, in Surah al-Nisa', describes that scene.

If they had referred the matter to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, it says, the ones among them able to draw it out would have known it. Draw it out. Some answers don't sit on the surface.
Someone has to go down after them, and the going down takes work, and training, and honesty about what you find. Today's word is that work.

teach.b: The word is ijtihad, striving, exerting yourself to the limit. In law it names a qualified scholar's full effort to reach a ruling from the sources.

Everything this block has laid out is the toolkit: the Qur'an, the sunnah, agreement, analogy, reason, the common good, custom. Ijtihad is the work of picking them up and using them on a real question.

Earlier in this block came a report in Sahih al-Bukhari about two judges who both strive: the one who gets it right has two rewards, and the one who misses has one. That striving has a name, and this is it.

Notice the word qualified. The one who does ijtihad, the mujtahid, is expected to know the Qur'an and the sunnah closely, to know Arabic well, to know where the scholars already agree, and to know the method.
That's why the reward for being wrong isn't a loophole for anyone with an opinion. It's for the person who did the work. And here the communities differ.
Some later Sunni writers spoke of the door of ijtihad as closed, with the great questions settled inside the schools; other Sunni scholars argued the door never closed.
Among Shia Muslims, living mujtahids remain at the center of religious life, and believers turn to them for rulings today. That's tomorrow.

how: Qualified jurists, known as mujtahids, derive rulings from the Qur'an, the sunnah and the other sources; Shia Muslims turn to living mujtahids, and Sunni scholars work largely within the established schools.

the Qur'an speaks of people able to draw out the meaning of a matter
in Surah al-Nisa', a matter referred to those in authority would be known by those able to draw it out.
all Muslims agree the door of ijtihad closed long ago

games.q: you're a trained jurist. a new question reaches you, and no verse, report or agreement names it. what do you do?
o: send it back to the Prophet.
strive with my own judgment and spare no effort.
games.why: that full effort, by someone qualified, is ijtihad. and in the report of the two judges, an honest miss after real effort still earns a reward.

practice: Pick one real question, small but honest: should I say yes to this, what do I owe this person?

Go in order, the way the schools teach it: what do the things I trust most say, what has someone wise already done, and only then, my own best judgment, with full effort. You may still get it wrong; the effort is the point.
